prediction:
THOUGHT: The history and exam point to a hereditary mechanobullous disorder with ectodermal and mucosal involvement. Key features: childhood-onset localized blistering with milia and nail dystrophy, congenital lacrimal duct obstruction, loss of eyebrows/eyelashes from early childhood, syndactyly, and severe bulbar urethral strictures requiring repeated urethroplasties. These findings are typical of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) or related ectodermal syndromes with mucosal scarring. Skin biopsy/EM shows a subepidermal (sublamina densa) split with lamina densa/hemidesmosomes on the roof and collagen bundles on the dermal base — a cleavage plane often seen with dermal-anchoring–fibril (dystrophic) EB but can be altered when basement membrane assembly is severely perturbed. Immunostaining shows mislocalized, low-intensity integrin α3 with normal integrin β1 and normal collagen XVII. Critically, whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous ITGA3 c.821G>A (p.R274Q) variant. ITGA3 encodes integrin α3 (α3β1), and pathogenic biallelic ITGA3 variants cause an autosomal recessive epidermolysis bullosa phenotype (integrin α3–deficient EB / ITGA3-related JEB), often with variable multi-organ involvement (historically grouped with ILNEB: interstitial lung disease, nephrotic syndrome, and EB), though expressivity can be mild and spare lung/kidney in some patients. The combination of clinical phenotype, integrin α3 mislocalization on IF, and a homozygous likely pathogenic ITGA3 variant makes ITGA3-related epidermolysis bullosa the most likely diagnosis. Other EB subtypes (especially dystrophic EB due to COL7A1) and junctional EB due to laminin-332 defects are reasonable differentials given the blister level and mucosal scarring but are less likely given the molecular result and the immunostaining pattern. Ectodermal dysplasia/p63-related syndromes can explain hair/nail/duct anomalies and syndactyly but do not fit the biopsy/genetics. Autoimmune subepidermal bullous diseases are unlikely given onset in childhood, congenital features, and genetic findings.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Junctional epidermolysis bullosa due to integrin α3 deficiency (ITGA3-related EB / ITGA3 homozygous p.R274Q) — most likely
2) Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (COL7A1-related) — possible given sublamina densa blistering, nail dystrophy, milia and mucosal strictures (less likely because ITGA3 variant identified and COL7A1 not implicated)
3) Junctional epidermolysis bullosa due to laminin-332 deficiency (LAMA3/LAMB3/LAMC2) — phenotypically overlapping JEB with mucosal/nail involvement (less likely given normal laminin-332–related markers and specific ITGA3 finding)
4) Ectodermal dysplasia / p63-related ectodermal syndromes (e.g., AEC/EEC spectrum) or ectodermal dysplasia–skin fragility syndromes — explain ectodermal and limb anomalies but do not match the biopsy/genetic data
5) Autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease (e.g., epidermolysis bullosa acquisita or mucous membrane pemphigoid) — unlikely in a teenager with congenital findings and a causal ITGA3 mutation, but included as a remote differential for subepidermal blistering.
ground_truth: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa with renal and respiratory involvement (junctional EB-RR), skin and mucosa-limited variant
